title: Given an unsorted array of numbers and a value K, find the K largest numbers. Explain why a min-heap of size K is the efficient structure and how it maintains the K largest seen so far.
shortTitle: Top K Numbers (Find the K Largest Numbers with a Min-Heap)

s1_definition.profdef: Top K Numbers is the foundational Top K Elements problem. We maintain a min-heap limited to size K. We push the first K numbers, then for each remaining number, if it is larger than the heap's smallest element, which is the root, we pop the root and push the new number. The heap always holds the K largest numbers seen so far, giving O(n log K) time.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, we want the K biggest transactions of the day from a long stream. We keep a small bucket that holds only the K biggest so far, where the smallest of those K sits at the top for quick checking. Each new transaction only enters the bucket if it beats the smallest one currently in it, pushing that smallest one out.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a min-heap of size K; a new number replaces the heap root only if it is bigger, so the heap always holds the K largest.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Top K Numbers is the foundational Top K Elements problem. We maintain a min-heap limited to size K. We push the first K numbers, then for each remaining number, if it is larger than the heap's smallest element, which is the root, we pop the root and push the new number. The heap always holds the K largest numbers seen so far, giving O(n log K) time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, we want the K biggest transactions of the day from a long stream. We keep a small bucket that holds only the K biggest so far, where the smallest of those K sits at the top for quick checking. Each new transaction only enters the bucket if it beats the smallest one currently in it, pushing that smallest one out.

**One line to remember:** Keep a min-heap of size K; a new number replaces the heap root only if it is bigger, so the heap always holds the K largest.

sections.s2_technical:
We use a `PriorityQueue<Integer>` as a min-heap, the default ordering in Java. We first offer the initial K elements so the heap fills to size K. Then for each remaining element we compare it with `minHeap.peek()`, the smallest of the current K: if the new element is larger we `poll()` the root and `offer()` the new element. For example, `if (num > minHeap.peek()) { minHeap.poll(); minHeap.offer(num); }`. At the end the heap contains exactly the K largest numbers.

The reason a min-heap of size K beats sorting is cost. Sorting the whole array is O(n log n); the min-heap approach is O(n log K), which is much smaller when K is small relative to n, and it uses only O(K) extra space. The smallest-at-the-root arrangement is what makes the keep-or-discard decision a single constant-time peek.

A senior nuance is that we want the K largest, so counter-intuitively we use a min-heap, not a max-heap, because the root being the smallest of the kept set lets us cheaply evict the weakest candidate. If we wanted the K smallest we would use a max-heap by symmetry. Complexity is O(n log K) time and O(K) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India processes a long stream of daily transaction amounts and the risk team wants only the K largest for a priority review, without sorting the entire stream. This is exactly how Top K Numbers works.

Problem 2 — Sorting every transaction to take the top K is wasteful when K is small. This is why we keep a min-heap of size K, where each new amount only displaces the smallest kept amount if it is larger, costing a cheap peek and an occasional heap operation.

The code defines a `TopTransactionsService` exposing `topK(amounts, k)` returning the K largest amounts. A `Demo` finds the top three transaction amounts and logs them.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: amounts 3200, 15000, 800, 9400, 22000, 1200, 7600 and K equal to 3.

Step 1: Seed the heap with the first three amounts 3200, 15000, 800; the root, the smallest, is 800.

Step 2: Next amount 9400 is greater than root 800, so pop 800 and push 9400; the heap now holds 3200, 15000, 9400 with root 3200.

Step 3: Next amount 22000 is greater than root 3200, so pop 3200 and push 22000; the heap holds 9400, 15000, 22000 with root 9400.

Step 4: Next amount 1200 is not greater than root 9400, so it is ignored. Next amount 7600 is not greater than root 9400, so it is ignored.

Step 5: The heap holds the three largest amounts 9400, 15000, 22000.


sections.s5b_flow:
```
  amounts stream, K=3
    │ seed heap with first 3 → root = smallest kept
    ▼
  for each next amount:
    ├─ amount > root → poll root, offer amount
    └─ else          → discard
    ▼
  heap = {9400, 15000, 22000}  (K largest)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Top K Numbers is the foundational Top K Elements problem, and the key counter-intuitive choice is that to find the K largest numbers I use a min-heap, not a max-heap. I keep the heap bounded to size K. I seed it with the first K numbers, and then for every remaining number I compare it against the heap's root, which is the smallest of the K numbers I am currently keeping. If the new number is larger I evict the root and insert the new number; if not I discard it.

The reason the min-heap works is that the root is always the weakest candidate in my kept set, so deciding whether a new number deserves a place is a single constant-time peek, and eviction is one heap operation. This gives n log K time and K space, which is far better than sorting the whole array at n log n when K is small.

At the National Bank of India I used this to pull the K largest transaction amounts from a long daily stream for the risk team's priority review, without sorting every transaction. I kept a size-K min-heap where each new amount only displaced the smallest kept amount if it was larger. Explaining why a min-heap rather than a max-heap gives the K largest, and the n log K versus n log n argument, is what shows an interviewer I understand the structure choice, not just the result.
